neighbours.label: ' broke' / ' breaking' / ' break' in the outbreak sense: a war, fire, fight or panic that 'breaks out' or 'breaks loose'. Other senses of break (a bone, a record, a window, 'broke down', 'broke up') stay quiet.
fire: The harvest was nearly finished when the civil war broke out in the north.
Investigators believe the blaze broke out in a storage room on the second floor.
A brawl broke out between rival supporters outside the stadium.
As soon as the verdict was read, pandemonium broke loose in the courtroom.
Clashes kept breaking out along the border throughout the winter.
Nobody was in the building when the fire broke out on Tuesday night.
Every few summers a new epidemic would break out in the crowded port.
Panic broke out on the lower deck when the lights failed.
quiet: The harvest was nearly finished when the old tractor broke down in the north field.
Investigators believe the burglar broke a window in a storage room on the second floor.
The goalkeeper broke two fingers during the match at the stadium.
As soon as the verdict was read, the reporters ran out of the courtroom.
The swimmer broke her own national record twice that winter.
The couple broke up shortly after moving into the building.
Every few summers a new ferry would start running from the crowded port.
The shelf broke under the weight of the books when the bracket failed.

notes: Card: ' broke' x15 of top 32, all 'broke out' / 'broke loose'; output promotes break/broke/erupt/burst. Probes: 'war broke out' 0.90, 'fire broke out' 0.85, 'all hell broke loose' 0.95, 'breaking out' 0.93; 'broke his wrist' 0.04, 'broke the record' 0.08, 'broke down' 0.06, 'broke into' 0.14, 'broke up' 0.06. The pole also fires weakly before the verb when an outbreak is coming ('A scuffle started' 0.30 on 'uffle', 'erupted' 0.22), so it reads as an 'outbreak' feature that peaks on break.
